data.title: As the AI model race heats up, who will come out on top?
data.description:
Companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to develop artificial intelligence models, hoping to establish technological advantages that could translate into lasting commercial returns. 

But as competitors release increasingly capable models within months of one another, investors face a difficult question: how sustainable is a strategy built around continuously spending more to stay ahead?

The rapid pace of innovation is creating opportunities for AI developers to attract users, win enterprise customers, and reshape established industries. 

However, the short shelf life of technological leadership raises questions about whether the revenue generated by successive model upgrades can justify the cost of developing them.

Meta's Muse has emerged as a prominent example of the commercial potential of AI.

More than 10 million people in the US and Canada had downloaded the Muse app, Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said during the company's earnings call last week.

The milestone is notable because ChatGPT's app took about three times as long to reach 10 million downloads, according to data from market-intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

Anthropic's Claude Cowork, meanwhile, triggered a sell-off in software stocks in February as investors worried that AI could undermine traditional software business models.

These developments demonstrate the technology's ability to attract users and challenge established industries. 

Yet user adoption and market disruption do not necessarily translate into sustainable profits for the companies financing the underlying technology.

As Anthropic filed its S-1 registration earlier this week, it revealed an operating loss of $693 million in the first half of 2026.

Results of big tech companies like Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon also revealed huge cash spending for AI buildout.

The heavy cash expenditure has resulted in stocks plunging on Friday as investors rotated out of artificial intelligence-related stocks.

As the AI race intensifies, it becomes more important for AI providers to generate sustainable revenue and not just release the most advanced model.

AI spending is rising faster than the certainty of returns

The scale of investment required to compete in the AI market is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

Goldman Sachs estimates that the largest US AI hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion in capital expenditure in 2026, with consensus forecasts pointing to $1.1 trillion in 2027.

The bank expects capital expenditure to increase further in 2027 and potentially exceed consensus estimates, although the pace of growth and the size of positive surprises are expected to diminish compared with recent quarters.

According to Goldman Sachs's equity analysts, hyperscalers will need to generate approximately $300 billion in annual AI revenue over the next few years to break even on their investments, based on average annual capital expenditure in 2026 and 2027.

There are reasons for optimism. Hyperscaler cloud revenues accelerated sharply in 2026, annualising approximately $70 billion above the pre-AI trend in the second quarter, while announced revenue backlogs exceeded $1.5 trillion.

Nevertheless, these figures do not eliminate the central uncertainty: how much of the revenue growth will translate into returns that adequately compensate companies and their investors for the cost and risk of the investments?

Alexander Lis, chief investment officer at investment firm SDV, believes the industry will need a substantial increase in sales to justify its spending.

"It is going to take massive additional revenues to justify the current aggregate CapEx levels of ~ $1.4 trillion per annum: from $5 trillion to $8 trillion in incremental sales (factoring in EBITDA margin and ROI assumptions)," Lis told Invezz.

He warned that the problem could emerge when investors begin to doubt whether such incremental sales are achievable.

For now, growing usage has helped compensate for falling token prices, he added. 

But Lis cautioned that “Should AI adoption decelerate, massive CapEx would start to be a problem.”

When a better model becomes a short-lived advantage

The financial challenge is not simply that AI development is expensive.

It is that a technological lead may not last long enough to justify the investment required to achieve it.

A company can spend billions developing a flagship model, only for a competitor to release a more capable or cheaper alternative a few months later. 

The first company's technological advantage may consequently have limited value if customers can switch to a rival offering comparable performance at a lower price.

A Bloomberg report citing The Epoch Capabilities Index said the top spot among AI models changed 20 times since 2024. 

A model has only remained as the frontier model for about seven weeks. That’s a very short time to be numero uno after spending billions of dollars. 

Ilman Shazhaev, Founder and CEO of Dizzaract, argues that the economics of pursuing a technological lead have already become questionable as a strategy for maintaining a competitive advantage.

"The core misconception behind 2026 capital spending of roughly $765 billion is mistaking high use for high value," Shazhaev told Invezz.

Even if lower prices encourage greater usage and keep computing clusters busy, high utilisation does not automatically translate into attractive margins.

Even if prices plunge and demand rises enough to fill clusters, a power plant runs at full capacity for its whole life and still makes utility margins. Meanwhile, hardware efficiency, algorithmic compression, and open-weight models matching closed frontier performance within four months trigger what I call the “Fixed-Capability Collapse.” This cuts the cost of serving a given level of intelligence roughly tenfold every year.

Founder and CEO of Dizzaract
Ilman Shazhaev

He argues that unless frontier workloads continue to require exponentially larger, tightly connected computing clusters, some of today's infrastructure could become economically outdated by 2030.

The risk is particularly significant because AI hardware does not retain its economic value indefinitely. 

Shazhaev estimates that AI accelerators could become obsolete within three to five years, while new chip generations arrive approximately every 12 months.

This creates a potential mismatch between the accounting treatment of expensive infrastructure and its actual economic usefulness.

Shazhaev estimates that the gap between accounting depreciation and economic reality could reach $176 billion between 2026 and 2028.

Open-ended models eating into closed-ended models’ lunch

Another threat for the top-end models is the cheaper open-ended models, which seem to be catching up to frontier models’ performance within months. 

Chinese developers and open-weight models are adding another layer of competition, challenging the pricing power of companies developing proprietary, closed models. 

As the performance gap narrows, customers have more reasons to consider alternatives that deliver comparable results at a fraction of the cost.

A Bloomberg News analysis found that Moonshot's Kimi K3 could build the same e-commerce website as Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 for one-fourth of the cost. 

The comparison shows how cheaper alternatives could erode the commercial advantage of expensive frontier models, especially for customers whose workloads don't require the most advanced capabilities.

The competitive pressure also extends beyond pricing. 

Open-weight models allow developers to access and adapt models' underlying weights, potentially giving businesses more flexibility in how they deploy AI. 

That could make them particularly attractive in markets where customers have limited budgets.

AI routing company OpenRouter said the five most popular models on its platform were Chinese, suggesting that affordability and accessibility can influence adoption alongside technical performance.

For US AI developers, the risk is that continued investment in building the most capable models may not translate into a proportionate commercial advantage if customers increasingly choose cheaper alternatives.

The pressure is already influencing pricing decisions at leading AI laboratories. 

In September, OpenAI and Anthropic introduced less expensive models as competition from open-weight alternatives intensified.

OpenAI added GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna to its GPT-6 family, cutting API prices by 50% compared with GPT-5.6 promotional pricing.

Anthropic, meanwhile, introduced Claude Opus 5.5, describing it as a more token-efficient model that would cost around 40% less to run than its Opus 5 predecessor.

These moves suggest that even established frontier-model developers are under pressure to improve cost efficiency rather than compete on performance alone.

Lower prices could help expand adoption and attract more customers, potentially supporting revenue growth through higher usage volumes.

However, they could also reduce the revenue earned per unit of AI processing, making it more difficult for companies to recover the costs of developing and operating their models.

Big Tech has a funding advantage, but capital alone may not be enough

The ability to finance the AI race is unevenly distributed.

Analysts said the large technology companies have established revenue streams, access to public markets, cloud businesses, and existing customer relationships. 

These advantages give them more flexibility to absorb high research and infrastructure costs than smaller, independent AI developers.

Lis said large technology incumbents are in a stronger position to fund the race because of their access to public markets. However, he questioned whether substantial investment necessarily creates a sustainable competitive advantage when rivals can offer comparable technology at much lower prices.

Shazhaev similarly argues that established technology companies are better equipped to absorb frontier-model training costs.

He added that “but as raw intelligence becomes commoditized, proprietary behavioral data and distribution matter far more than capital or hardware.”

In his view, control over computing hardware can provide a temporary advantage, but it cannot necessarily prevent competitors from reproducing similar capabilities through other models.

Pure-play AI laboratories face a different challenge.

Without diversified businesses generating substantial cash flows, they may have to rely more heavily on venture capital, strategic investors, and other financing sources.

Shazhaev pointed to the large funding requirements of leading AI laboratories and the possibility that public listings could shift more of the financial risk onto public-market investors.

What are sustainable revenue avenues for AI companies?

If the advantage from a superior model is temporary, companies need other ways to protect their returns.

During the last technology revolutions, the greatest beneficiaries were the ones that figured out how to use technology to strengthen their products, improve productivity, or distance themselves from competitors (like streaming and gaming companies vs. telecoms during the internet boom). From this point of view, proprietary data sets and strong distribution networks matter more than access to cheap capital.

Chief investment officer at investment firm SDV
Alexander Lis

Rather than spending continually to outperform every rival on model benchmarks, a company can build products around customer needs, integrate AI into established workflows and use specialised information to deliver results that competitors cannot easily replicate.

Shazhaev makes a similar case, arguing that “companies escape the leapfrog cycle when they treat models as parts they can swap and build their edge in layers that stay scarce: workflow integration, simulated testing worlds, low-cost distributed delivery, and smart allocation that keeps customers.”

He draws a distinction between a high valuation or a temporary revenue surge and a durable business.

“Fast revenue helps short-term fundraising, but when open-weight models deliver frontier performance four months later at a fraction of the cost, customers churn unless your software is deeply woven into their daily work.”

The same principle applies to AI applications in financial services, healthcare, cybersecurity and industrial automation, where specialised knowledge, proprietary data and regulatory requirements may help companies establish defensible positions.

For investors, this means evaluating whether AI spending creates measurable economic benefits rather than treating model performance or user growth as sufficient evidence of commercial success.

The race to develop superior models may also create opportunities for businesses that support AI deployment rather than compete directly in model development.

Ryan Kirkley, chief executive and co-founder of Global Settlement Network, said “I think the economics become questionable when companies are spending billions to maintain a technological advantage that lasts six months, particularly if that advantage doesn't translate into customers willing to pay a premium.”

He expects a handful of companies to continue developing frontier models while the broader commercial opportunity expands into the infrastructure supporting AI applications.

Michael Heinrich, chief executive and co-founder of 0G Labs, similarly argued that “As intelligence gets cheaper, the scarce thing becomes proof: that the model you paid for is the one that ran, that your data stayed private, and that an agent did what it was told. I expect durable value to sit with whoever can supply that proof at scale.”

The post As the AI model race heats up, who will come out on top? appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Big tech names remain attractive - not their stocks though
data.description:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom still offers an investment opportunity – but Bank of America’s senior strategist Michael Hartnett believes the better deal now lies in lending to technology giants rather than owning their shares.

As of October 30th, he views selected Magnificent Seven bonds yielding 6% to 8% as increasingly attractive after a bruising selloff.

His argument turns the AI investment narrative on its head: companies spending aggressively to build tomorrow’s infrastructure could reward creditors even while testing shareholders’ patience.

The distinction matters as financing costs climb and cash demands intensify.

AI’s enormous funding bill changes the investment equation

The pressure is visible in Amazon’s latest earnings.

The company maintained its $220 billion capex forecast for 2026 while reporting $42.4 billion in negative free cash flow in the trailing 12 months.

Yet operating cash flow increased 29% to $168.3 billion.

That combination reveals the underlying problem: Amazon’s operations are producing substantial cash – but its infrastructure investments are consuming even more.

For shareholders, the “uncertainty” concerns when that spending will generate sufficient additional returns.

But bondholders face a different calculation: whether the borrower can meet interest payments and repay principal.

A business can remain creditworthy while delivering disappointing stock returns.

Hartnett’s preference therefore reflects a distinction between corporate financial strength and the price investors pay to participate in future growth.

Meta’s financing shift offers creditors a different signal

Hartnett’s figures put hyperscaler debt issuance at $182 billion this year, alongside $89 billion in equity issuance – a combined $271 billion.

That funding appetite helps explain why investors are demanding more compensation to finance the AI expansion.

Meta’s plan to raise up to $95 billion through stock offerings illustrates how the consequences can differ across investors.

Additional common shares can dilute existing ownership, while equity financing can reduce reliance on further borrowing, potentially supporting creditors.

The package includes different securities, so its ultimate effect depends on the terms and execution.

Hartnett interprets the shift as evidence that the “era of big buybacks is over.”

That is his broader market thesis, rather than a declaration that every technology company will stop repurchasing shares.

Attractive yields still require careful bond selection

The appeal is straightforward: investors buying selected bonds at depressed prices can secure higher yields and potentially benefit if prices recover.

Unlike shareholders, they do not need expanding stock valuations to earn their contractual payments.

However, a quoted 6% to 8% yield is neither a universal offer across technology debt nor a guaranteed annual investment return.

Maturity, purchase price, seniority, and the issuing entity all matter.

Longer-dated securities can fall sharply when market interest rates rise, while deteriorating credit conditions can push prices lower even if Treasury yields decline.

Hartnett’s thesis ultimately rests on whether borrowing costs now compensate investors adequately for those risks.

For investors convinced that leading technology companies will remain financially resilient, their bonds offer a way to participate in the AI financing cycle with a different balance of income, upside, and downside exposure.

data.title: Nasdaq plunges 2.8% as Intel and Amazon results deepen AI stock sell-off
data.description:
US stocks fell sharply on Friday, with the Nasdaq Composite recording its largest one-day percentage decline since June 5 as disappointing results from Intel and Amazon intensified concerns about the returns on massive artificial intelligence investments.

The technology-heavy index dropped 2.86% to 25,437, while the S&P 500 declined 1.82% to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.09% to 51,770.31.

Selling pressure spread across semiconductor stocks and major technology companies as investors reassessed the outlook for AI-related spending.

The declines also reflected concerns about whether companies can generate sufficient returns from the infrastructure being built to support the technology.

All three major indexes ended the week lower. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq also recorded monthly losses in October, while the Dow finished the month higher.

Intel and Amazon results weigh on technology stocks

Intel shares plunged around 29% after the chipmaker issued a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below analysts' estimates of $17.1 billion.

The forecast followed third-quarter adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, ahead of expectations of 40 cents.

Revenue reached $16.51 billion, slightly above the $16.5 billion consensus estimate.

Amazon also came under pressure after reporting third-quarter earnings and revenue that missed Wall Street expectations.

The company reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion and maintained its 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $220 billion.

The weakness extended across the semiconductor sector.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index recorded a monthly loss, while Advanced Micro Devices fell 11%. Nvidia and Broadcom declined 4% and 5%, respectively.

SanDisk lost 13%, despite reporting better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results.

The broader technology sell-off also affected AI infrastructure companies.

CoreWeave shares fell more than 37% in October, while Nebius posted a monthly decline of 34%. The Roundhill Memory ETF, which includes Micron and Seagate Technology, lost 20% during the month.

Investors reassess AI spending and returns

The latest declines reflect growing scrutiny of the financial commitments behind the AI boom.

Investors are increasingly focused on whether large technology companies and infrastructure providers can translate substantial capital expenditure into sustainable returns.

Alphabet shares recorded their worst day on record on Thursday after missing third-quarter earnings and revenue expectations and reporting negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion.

Meanwhile, concerns about financing have weighed on neocloud companies that provide computing infrastructure for AI data centres.

CoreWeave has faced rising bond yields, adding to investor concerns about debt levels across the sector.

Reports that Blackstone told investors Anthropic may not receive an investment-grade credit rating after its planned market debut also added to the pressure.

The shift in sentiment has prompted investors to move away from some technology stocks and towards more defensive sectors.

Consumer staples and healthcare shares advanced on Friday, with Walmart and Coca-Cola each gaining more than 1%. Merck and Amgen also rose.

October ends with mixed performance across Wall Street

Despite Friday's losses, third-quarter corporate earnings have remained broadly positive.

Of the 299 S&P 500 companies that had reported results, 82% exceeded consensus expectations, according to LSEG data.

Analysts now expect S&P 500 earnings to grow 31.6% year over year in the quarter.

Energy companies Exxon Mobil and Chevron also beat quarterly profit expectations, benefiting from higher refining margins amid energy supply disruptions linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine.

However, the technology-led weakness weighed on the broader monthly performance.

The Nasdaq was heading towards a 5% October decline, its steepest monthly fall since March 2025. The S&P 500 was on track to lose less than 1%, while the Dow was poised to gain around 2%.

data.title: Why Nvidia shares are down over 4% on Friday?
data.description:
Nvidia NVDA shares fell sharply on Friday as a broad selloff in technology stocks intensified concerns over the cost of artificial intelligence infrastructure and the time required for companies to generate returns on their investments.

Disappointing results from Amazon and Intel weighed on semiconductor stocks, while fresh reports involving CEO Jensen Huang and regulatory scrutiny of the company's acquisition plans added to the spotlight on the chipmaker.

Nvidia was down more than 4.8% trading around $203.40 at the time of writing.

The wider market was also under pressure, with the Nasdaq Composite falling nearly 2.5%, while the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average also traded lower.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped around 7% as losses spread across chipmakers.

Amazon and Intel results deepen AI concerns

Amazon's third-quarter results added to investor unease over the scale of spending required to build AI infrastructure.

The company reported a trailing 12-month free cash flow outflow of $42.4 billion, compared with a positive $14.8 billion in the year-earlier period. It was largely driven by increased investment in property and equipment, primarily for AI.

Amazon maintained its capital expenditure outlook of approximately $220 billion for 2026, reinforcing concerns over how quickly its investments will translate into stronger cash generation.

Its shares also came under pressure following the results.

Intel's weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter guidance further unsettled the chip sector.

Although the company beat third-quarter earnings estimates, it forecast revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion for the current quarter, below Wall Street's expectation of around $17 billion. Its adjusted earnings forecast of 25 cents per share also missed the consensus estimate of approximately 43 cents.

Intel shares plunged nearly 29%, while AMD dropped around 10%, adding to the pressure on Nvidia and other semiconductor companies.

Alphabet's results had already contributed to the technology selloff a day earlier.

The Google parent reported third-quarter free cash flow of negative $9.07 billion as capital expenditure on AI infrastructure climbed, while weaker-than-expected advertising revenue added to investor concerns.

Report raises questions over Jensen Huang's contact

Separately, a New York Times report published Thursday said US intelligence agencies had concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, an executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, was allegedly acting as a Chinese intelligence asset and passing commercial information to Beijing.

The report said surveillance had revealed that she developed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia rejected suggestions that the interactions were unusual, saying meetings with customers were part of the CEO's job.

The company also said regional cloud customers received ordinary business information, not sensitive trade secrets or information relevant to national security.

DOJ questions Nvidia's Hugging Face deal

Nvidia is also facing questions from the US Department of Justice over its proposed $12.93 billion acquisition of open-source AI platform Hugging Face.

Reuters reported that the department has asked whether the deal could give Nvidia control over an important distribution channel for AI and provide leverage over competitors.

The inquiry forms part of a broader examination of Nvidia's acquisitions, investments and sales practices.

The DOJ's questions do not establish wrongdoing or mean that legal action will necessarily follow.

data.title: Column: A hawkish Fed, shaky tech and the risk of an earnings letdown
data.description:
Markets are now heading into the last two months of the year, having closed out October with a flurry of significant events.

First off, the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, and Bank of Japan all held monetary policy meetings in the final week of October, and interest rates were left unchanged, as expected.

That removes a potential short-term headwind for equities.

Yet there’s still a general expectation that central banks will tighten monetary policy before the year-end, due to stubbornly high inflation.

Focusing on the US, the CME’s FedWatch Tool puts the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in early December at around 70%.

And if it once again chooses to leave rates on hold through to the year-end, then there’s less than a 10% chance that it won’t have hiked by mid-March 2027.

The interesting thing is that markets were more hawkish before the Fed meeting than after.

This is despite two FOMC members voting for an increase on Wednesday. Some observers considered that choice to be performative.

That could be the case, knowing that the majority wanted to hold, and given the problems that another hike would cause coming just a few days before the dreaded midterms – more in a minute.

But when it comes to pricing pressures, who can blame them? The major inflation updates released earlier this month were horrible.

September Core and Headline CPI both came in way above expectations and the prior month’s readings, with Headline being the highest number year-on-year since May.

Following this, the PPI data (the key measure of wholesale inflation, which typically leads consumer prices) proved to be even more shocking, with Core and Headline hitting highs last seen nearly four years ago.

To top it all, the day after the Fed left rates on hold, Core PCE, still the Fed’s preferred inflation measure and the one used for its 2% target, ticked up to 3.1% from 3.0%.

Not only is it moving in the wrong direction, but the last time it was below the Fed’s target rate was in February 2021.

Perhaps the Fed is hoping that a new virus will come and do its job for it again.

Failing that, if the tech sector selloff accelerates from here, the Fed could soon be cutting rather than hiking.

Bear in mind, the Fed, under its newish Chair Kevin Warsh, has made it clear that it will now be led by the data, rather than guiding the markets to a preordained route for monetary policy.

It has also said that getting inflation back down to its 2% target remains its number one priority.

Yet there was a dismal Non-Farm Payroll update in early October, along with an unwelcome uptick in the Unemployment Rate.

And it’s not the first time that payrolls have disappointed since the summer.

This has led some observers to wonder about the underlying health of the US economy once growth from the AI infrastructure buildout is subtracted.

That’s not to say that the AI trade isn’t genuine, only that it is highly concentrated and in danger of unravelling if certain optimistic assumptions don’t play out as currently priced.

And that brings us to the third quarter earnings season.

Earnings growth has been the biggest tailwind for US equity markets for years now.

And it is expected to continue into this quarter as well, with a year-on-year earnings growth rate forecast around 30%.

That could well come to pass. But results from Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon have really put the skids under the hyperscaler trade.

Meanwhile, and ahead of the upcoming Anthropic IPO, the only listed frontier lab, SpaceX, is trading at its lowest level in two months.

The chip sector looks like a bloodbath, and neoclouds aren’t looking particularly perky either.

Who knows how this will play out. Another ‘buy the dip’ opportunity?

Investors are now preparing for the midterm elections on the 3rd of November.

History shows that what happens after midterm elections has little overall effect on US stock market performance.

Corporate earnings, economic growth, employment, inflation and interest rates tend to matter far more.

Despite this, there have been times when politically sensitive sectors such as energy, healthcare and tech have faced different degrees of scrutiny following a change in control of Congress.

That can lead to a period of sector rotation, rather than the whole market moving one way.

Aside from this, a look at past midterms shows that political gridlock is a common outcome, and that often goes down well with financial markets.

The president’s party usually loses seats, and a split government is often seen as placing a limit on what an administration can do.

That could be considered a significant issue in the current political environment.

The polls close on the 3rd of November, and prediction markets suggest that a Republican-controlled Senate and a Democrat-controlled House are the most likely outcome.

This will be both an annoyance and a constraint for President Trump.

But it won’t affect his ability to issue executive orders, as well as deciding much of trade and foreign policy, including going to war.

So, as October draws to a close, the biggest challenge remains beating lofty earnings expectations. What could possibly go wrong?

(This is a fortnightly column by David Morrison. He is a Senior Market Analyst at Trade Nation. Views are his own.)

data.title: Big Tech's AI bill meets a 'Big Cash Burn' issue: are investors' fears justified?
data.description:
Cash burn emerged as a key metric for investors assessing Big Tech earnings this season, as companies ramp up spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure while borrowing costs remain elevated.

Results from major technology companies over the past two weeks intensified concerns about whether the billions of dollars being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough to justify the investment.

Investors were seen increasingly distinguishing between companies that can finance their expansion through operating cash flow and those whose spending is putting pressure on their balance sheets.

Microsoft was rewarded for demonstrating that it can fund its ambitions without continuously tapping capital markets.

Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, meanwhile, faced pressure as their expanding infrastructure budgets weigh on free cash flow.

More than $2 trillion in market value is set to be wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 this month, according to Reuters, as investors reassess the sustainability of the AI investment boom.

Alphabet, Amazon and Meta face cash flow pressure

Alphabet's latest results highlighted the growing tension between AI investment and the financial performance of its established businesses.

Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, demonstrating strong demand for AI-related services.

However, the company's free cash flow turned negative by $9.07 billion, substantially worse than the $2.70 billion analysts had expected.

Investors were also concerned about slowing growth in Google Search, which remains the company's largest source of revenue and helps finance its AI expansion.

Search advertising growth slowed for a third consecutive quarter and missed analyst expectations, while YouTube advertising revenue also came in below estimates.

Alphabet shares plunged 13% on Thursday, wiping out approximately $500 billion in market value in its worst single-day decline.

Amazon also came under pressure after reporting a substantial cash outflow despite delivering strong growth at its cloud computing business.

The company burned $42.4 billion on a trailing 12-month basis in the September quarter, driven by capital expenditure of $77.26 billion, around $20 billion above estimates, according to LSEG data.

This compared with cash burn of $7.6 billion in the previous quarter and positive free cash flow of $14.8 billion in the year-earlier period.

Amazon Web Services revenue increased 39% to $46 billion, beating expectations for growth of 38.2%.

However, the strong cloud performance did little to offset concerns about the company's spending commitments and weaker retail outlook.

"The free cash flow looks like the ugly part of the report," said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors in a Reuters report.

"Operations generated plenty of cash but their capex just absolutely swallowed it."

"The trend is pretty steep and pretty negative, and that's the big thing that is alarming in this report."

Amazon has forecast capital expenditure of $220 billion for this year as it expands its AI infrastructure and develops related services.

Its shares fell around 2% on Friday.

Meta has also faced investor scrutiny after reporting negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter.

The company raised the lower end of its full-year capital expenditure forecast to $135 billion from $130 billion, while maintaining the upper end at $145 billion.

Microsoft stands out with stronger cash generation

Microsoft offered a contrasting picture, demonstrating that substantial AI investment does not necessarily have to come at the expense of cash generation.

The company reported 48% growth in its Azure cloud business in the fiscal first quarter ended September and generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow, approximately $10 billion above analyst expectations.

The results provided evidence that its investments in AI infrastructure and cloud capacity are translating into stronger business growth while leaving sufficient cash to support further expansion.

"Across all four hyperscalers, we saw there is growth in the cloud business and in demand for AI tools. But in terms of running the business of the business, Microsoft seems to be the only one that's able to do all of this and still (generate cash) at the same time," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, in a Reuters report.

The difference is also reflected in their financing activities.

While Microsoft has started raising capital through debt, its issuance has been considerably smaller than that of some competitors this year.

Google has raised more than $140 billion through debt and equity offerings, while Meta has raised $62.5 billion and Amazon has garnered $98 billion through bond deals.

With interest rates making borrowing more expensive, companies that depend heavily on external financing could face greater pressure to demonstrate that their investments are generating adequate returns.

Core businesses also face growth challenges

Another concern for investors is that the enormous spending commitments are coinciding with signs of weakness in some of the companies' established businesses.

Amazon reported slower growth in both its retail and advertising operations.

Online sales increased 2% year over year, down from 10% growth a year earlier and below analyst expectations.

Its fourth-quarter revenue guidance also disappointed, with the midpoint falling below analysts' estimate of $244.5 billion, despite the period including the holiday shopping season.

Alphabet's search business has also shown signs of slowing as competition from ChatGPT, Claude and other AI-powered chatbots and agents intensifies.

Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter

The company has to invest heavily in AI while protecting the search business that has historically funded much of its expansion.

These developments have raised questions about whether AI-related growth can compensate for potential pressure on legacy revenue streams.

What experts say about the FCF issue

According to a Morgan Stanley report, companies create value when they invest in projects that generate returns above their cost of capital — the minimum return investors expect for providing funds.

In such cases, the future free cash flows (FCF) generated by the investments more than offset their initial cost, increasing the overall value of the business.

“In other words, a company with opportunities that promise sufficient returns should invest in all of them because those investments create value,” wrote Michael J. Mauboussin and Dan Callahan, CFA.

The report cited Walmart’s financial performance between 1973 and 1986 to illustrate this principle.

The retailer recorded negative free cash flow in each of those 14 years, but its average annual return on invested capital (ROIC) was 18%, comfortably above its cost of capital.

“Walmart created value by investing more than it earned. That paid off, as the stock produced an annual total shareholder return of 33 percent during that period, three times that of the S&P 500,” they said.

Hence, some strategists believe the recent sell-off reflects a period of reassessment rather than a fundamental deterioration in the technology sector.

Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James Investment Management, said the underlying fundamentals remained strong, even as investor positioning in technology stocks became increasingly crowded.

"Our playbook this year has been not to chase a lot of these trades higher, but really to use downside opportunistically," Orton said in an interview with CNBC.

He also argued that negative free cash flow at major technology companies could be temporary as they invest in capacity to meet rising demand.

Orton said he is "generally okay with these companies turning into negative free cash flow territory because it's going to be a temporary period."

Other investors are also less concerned about the cash burn at established technology companies, arguing that their existing businesses and balance sheets provide a cushion that smaller AI companies lack.

Christopher Ballard, a managing director at Check Capital Management, said Alphabet's negative free cash flow of around $9 billion was relatively small compared with its overall business, with operating income exceeding $40 billion in the quarter.

Unlike AI model developers OpenAI and Anthropic, which remain unprofitable and spend billions of dollars on infrastructure, Alphabet has an established business and a strong balance sheet, he said.

“They’re borrowing from the for-now in order to invest in the future,” Ballard said.

“I think it’s OK, and they’re doing it in a responsible manner.”

The contrasting views underline the debate facing investors.

While Big Tech companies may have the financial resources to sustain heavy AI investment for now, markets are increasingly demanding evidence that the spending will produce durable growth and sufficient cash returns to finance the next phase of expansion.

data.title: A Fed pause, a confusing message, and a December dilemma
data.description:
The Federal Reserve’s decision to hold interest rates steady was widely anticipated.

What proved harder to interpret was the message from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who reiterated that inflation remained too high but declined to indicate whether policymakers were preparing to raise rates again in December.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 on Wednesday to leave the federal funds target range unchanged at 3.75%-4%.

Fed governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring an immediate quarter-point increase.

The statement upgraded its description of economic activity from “solid” to “strong”, citing resilient domestic spending, robust capital investment and productivity growth, while saying inflation “remains elevated”.

It added that “the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”.

The wording left room for another increase, but did not commit the committee to one.

Warsh was similarly unwilling to signal the next move.

Asked whether there was still broad support for another increase this year, he said: “I don't believe in forward guidance absent exigent circumstances, absent a crisis.”

Markets initially priced an 84.6% probability of a quarter-point hike after Thursday's PCE release, but the odds had fallen to around 73% by Friday.

Was the pause more hawkish or dovish?

For Rebecca Homkes, an Economist and Lecturer at London Business School, the meeting met expectations on the decision but still left investors frustrated by the explanation.

“This week’s Fed meeting managed to somehow meet expectations and still induce frustrations,” Homkes said.

“While the no movement was firmly priced in, Warsh’s brief statements could be interpreted as inconsistent,” she told Invezz.

“So while the outcome was expected, guidance as to what data might inform a further hike would have been welcome. Despite talking tough on inflation and the Fed’s role in bringing it down, no urgency in getting to it was evident.”

She characterised the Fed as “talking tough on inflation but acting dovish that the economy can’t take much”.

She warned that the Fed risked falling behind the curve if it did not act while the data were pointing towards persistent price pressures.

JoAnne Bianco, Senior Investment Strategist at BondBloxx, offered a different reading.

She said the meeting should not be interpreted as a dovish shift because Warsh reiterated that inflation remained above target and that the committee was prepared to tighten further if necessary.

"The Fed held rates steady, but I do not think the meeting should be interpreted as a dovish shift," Bianco told Invezz.

She added that Warsh’s acknowledgement that financial conditions had tightened did not mean policymakers considered them restrictive.

During the presser, the chair said conditions had tightened for some businesses and households since September, but added: “I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight.”

Warsh described the effects of the September increase as beginning to filter through credit availability and borrowing costs, but did not say they had removed the need for further action.

Asked why the Fed had not raised rates immediately when inflation remained above target, Warsh said price stability was not a matter of “some fixed individual date on a calendar” or “some isolated data point”.

Did political considerations influence the decision?

The meeting came six days before the US midterm elections, prompting a question about whether politics had influenced the decision.

Warsh insisted politics played no role in the decision, saying he “didn't hear an utterance about politics” or any reference to the upcoming elections during the committee's two-day deliberations.

Robert R. Johnson, Professor of Finance at Creighton University’s Heider College of Business, said he believed the approaching elections were a contributing factor.

"While Warsh denied that politics played any role, I believe that the central bank wanted to show that it operates without political influence," Johnson told Invezz.

"It will be much easier to raise rates in December and avoid criticism that any decision was politically motivated."

Homkes said she did not believe politics had played a role, although she argued that inflation would have had to be considerably more severe to prompt a move immediately before the vote.

September PCE keeps inflation concerns alive

The latest inflation figures offered little evidence of a meaningful cooling in price pressures.

The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.5% in September from a month earlier, up from 0.3% in August, while the annual rate accelerated to 3.6% from 3.4%.

Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% monthly and 3.1% annually, compared with 3.0% in August.

Both the monthly and annual readings were broadly in line with economists' expectations.

David Russell, Global Head of Market Strategy at TradeStation Group, said earlier consumer and producer price releases had already pointed to uncomfortable inflation readings.

He said the latest PCE report did not move the needle because markets had already seen elevated readings on CPI, PPI and import and export prices.

Bianco said the figures reinforced the uneven nature of progress on inflation but did not materially change her December outlook.

Johnson said the report provided another data point supporting a rate increase.

What could change the December decision?

Russell said a December hike remained his base case because inflation was above target while the economy and labour market remained strong.

He said a single weak jobs report was unlikely to alter market expectations, adding that “a credible decline in energy prices might be the only catalyst that could meaningfully impact interest rates”.

Russell told Invezz that the Fed could not indefinitely dismiss supply-side inflation pressures if they persisted and spread into other prices.

“But these pressures get passed through when they last,” he said.

“Core CPI doesn’t exist to ignore inflation. It exists to look past short-term noise, and $6 diesel is no longer short-term noise.”

Bianco said weaker labour-market data, slowing consumer demand or further tightening in financial conditions could reduce the probability of a December increase.

A broader pattern of moderating growth and easing inflation, she added, would make the Fed more comfortable holding rates steady.

Homkes said a December hike was likely after the latest growth and inflation data, and that it would take a combination of weaker jobs, cooler inflation and signs of a slowdown to change that assessment.

Johnson also expected another increase, saying data showing a slowdown in inflation could alter the Fed’s thinking, although he did not see that as likely.

MUFG’s US Macro Strategy team is less convinced that a hike is imminent.

In its October 28 FOMC recap, the bank put the probability of a December increase at 55%, compared with market pricing of roughly 80% at the time.

It said the decision was “not a done deal” and that the outlook could change with incoming data, financial conditions, inflation expectations and the election.

For markets, the challenge is identifying what evidence the Fed will consider decisive when Warsh has made clear he does not intend to prejudge the next meeting.

Until the next round of employment and inflation data arrives, a December hike may remain the central expectation—but not a settled outcome.

data.title: Evening digest: Binance hack rattles crypto, oil rises
data.description:
Cryptocurrency markets and technology stocks came under pressure on Friday as the $6.3 billion Binance hack renewed concerns about digital asset security, while oil prices climbed amid escalating tensions in the Middle East.

Gold and other precious metals also fell sharply as investors reassessed the outlook for technology stocks and interest rates.

Meanwhile, Intel shares plunged after the chipmaker issued a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the fourth quarter.

Binance hack: $6.3B crypto theft rattles markets

The $6.3 billion Binance hack has renewed concerns about cryptocurrency exchange security, triggering a broader sell-off in digital assets and crypto-related stocks.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said approximately $3 billion of the stolen funds had been frozen on-chain with the help of blockchain partners.

The exchange has pledged to cover customer losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.

Teng attributed the breach to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allegedly allowed attackers to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

Binance said it had found no evidence of a private-key leak.

The incident also weighed on cryptocurrency-linked equities.

Coinbase shares fell more than 10%, reaching levels last seen in February 2024.

Circle Internet Group declined 9.5%, while Strategy lost 7.84%.

Bitcoin fell as much as 4.8% over 24 hours to approximately $76,820.

The attack has also raised questions about how stolen cryptocurrency can be recovered.

Stablecoin issuers, including Tether and Circle, have frozen funds associated with receiving addresses, while Bitcoin and Ethereum cannot be frozen through an equivalent issuer-controlled mechanism.

Binance has said customer balances remain safe and that it will cover the losses.

Investors will now watch the resumption of withdrawals and the exchange's updated proof-of-reserves report.

Oil prices: Brent settles above $117 as Iran war tensions intensify

Oil prices climbed more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders assessed the risk of further escalation in the Iran war.

Brent crude futures for December delivery settled 2.32% higher at $117.55 a barrel.

The contract touched an intraday high of $118 before expiring on Friday.

The more actively traded January Brent contract gained 1.56% to $112.53.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 1.11%, to settle at $103.13.

For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI advanced 15.2%.

Supply concerns intensified after a tanker was struck by explosive devices attached by a small boat in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency.

The incident highlighted risks to shipping through the strategic waterway, a major route for Gulf crude and fuel supplies.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed attacks on Saudi oil facilities, including the Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and a production facility in Abqaiq.

Gold price: Precious metals slide as technology stocks sell off

Gold prices fell to their lowest levels in a year on Friday, while silver, platinum and palladium also recorded substantial losses.

Spot gold dropped 3.44% to $3,881.68 an ounce, its lowest level since October 2025.

US gold futures for December delivery settled 3.46% lower at $3,891.10.

Silver fell 5.8% to $49.33 an ounce, breaking below the $50 level for the first time in 11 months. Platinum declined 3.68% to $1,438.50, while palladium lost 3% to $976.08.

The sell-off coincided with a sharp decline in technology stocks as concerns about the returns on artificial intelligence investments weighed on market sentiment.

Gold has now declined approximately 30% from its January record high of $5,595, amid expectations of higher interest rates for longer and weaker demand in Asia.

Intel shares plunge as weak Q4 forecast raises concerns

Intel shares plunged 28% in trading on Friday after the chipmaker issued a disappointing fourth-quarter revenue outlook.

The company expects December-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below analysts' expectations of $17.1 billion.

The forecast followed third-quarter adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, beating estimates of 40 cents.

Revenue reached $16.51 billion, slightly above the consensus estimate of $16.5 billion.

Intel also expects PC chip revenue to decline in the mid-20% range in the fourth quarter, following a 5% drop in the September quarter.

Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said the weakness in the PC market could persist into the first half of next year.

BofA Securities downgraded Intel to Neutral from Buy and cut its price target to $100 from $145.

Roth Capital also lowered its rating to Neutral and reduced its target to $70 from $120.

Analysts cited manufacturing constraints, weaker PC demand and competitive pressures as concerns.

However, Intel's expanding data-centre business and foundry ambitions remain potential longer-term growth drivers.

The post Evening digest: Binance hack rattles crypto, oil rises appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Anthropic IPO: Blackstone warns AI firm may receive junk credit rating: report
data.description:
Anthropic may struggle to secure an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its planned initial public offering, potentially increasing borrowing costs as the artificial intelligence company prepares for massive infrastructure spending.

Blackstone has told investors in Anthropic's latest $63 billion chip financing deal that the AI company is likely to receive a high-yield, or junk, credit rating following its IPO, said a Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter.

The assessment marks a shift from Blackstone's earlier guidance that Anthropic could secure an investment-grade rating before the end of the year.

Blackstone is an anchor investor in the financing arrangement, known as Project North Star, and is working with banks involved in distributing the debt to other investors.

Anthropic filed to go public on Monday, potentially setting up one of the largest stock market listings next month.

Its prospectus outlined plans to spend more than $800 billion on computing infrastructure between now and 2045.

Anthropic's potential junk rating raises financing concerns

Blackstone has recently indicated that Anthropic is more likely to receive a rating in the double-B range or above, based on guidance from major credit rating agencies, the people cited in the report said.

A double-B rating falls below investment grade and could restrict the company's access to institutional capital.

Many insurance companies and pension funds face restrictions on taking large positions in borrowers with junk-rated debt.

This could reduce the pool of investors available to finance Anthropic's infrastructure expansion.

Consequently, the company may need to continue relying on suppliers with stronger credit ratings to support its borrowing arrangements.

An investment-grade rating is important to Anthropic's long-term financing strategy because it would allow the company to access debt at relatively lower interest rates.

Anthropic currently has more than $112 billion in cash and equivalents.

Investors also anticipate that the company could raise approximately $100 billion through its IPO.

A US technology-focused portfolio manager told the Financial Times that credit access was central to the company's financing ambitions.

Project North Star relies on Broadcom's credit backing

The financing concerns come as banks have completed the $63 billion Project North Star deal, which provides funding for Anthropic to lease 1.5 gigawatts of Google's semiconductors.

More than $42 billion of the senior loans is guaranteed by Broadcom, which co-develops the chips and holds an investment-grade credit rating.

The remaining $18 billion in junior debt is backed by Anthropic's lease payments.

Senior debt generally takes priority over junior loans in the event of a default, making it more attractive to institutional investors.

Broadcom's high A-tier credit rating was an important factor in helping Anthropic secure the financing.

Blackstone's funds invested $9 billion in the junior debt at a yield of more than 10%, according to the Financial Times.

Rating agencies assign different assessments to Anthropic debt

Project North Star's $18 billion junior debt has received a double-B-plus rating with a positive outlook from Kroll Bond Rating Agency (KBRA).

This represents a modest improvement from the stable outlook assigned to a similar financing arrangement, Project Big Sky, four months earlier.

Morningstar DBRS also assigned the junior debt a double-B rating, according to people familiar with the matter.

However, Fitch, Moody's and S&P, the three major credit rating agencies with significant influence over corporate borrowing costs, have not officially issued credit ratings for Anthropic.

Bankers representing Anthropic and rival OpenAI have reportedly lobbied major rating agencies to award the AI companies investment-grade ratings following their respective IPOs.

The uncertainty surrounding Anthropic's credit outlook also coincided with broader weakness in technology stocks.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 3.84% in afternoon trading on Friday following an earlier sell-off triggered by concerns about the sustainability of AI spending.

As Anthropic gets closer to its public market debut, investors need to watch out for the credit ratings the company receives, as they will determine its debt load in funding its AI buildout.

data.title: Rivian stock rises as analysts back R2 outlook after Q3 earnings beat
data.description:
Rivian Automotive shares RIVN rose on Friday after the electric vehicle maker reported better-than-expected third-quarter results and raised its full-year delivery guidance.

Analysts highlighted the R2 electric SUV, improving production prospects, and the company's autonomous driving technology as potential growth drivers.

Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) shares gained 4.76% at the time of writing, marking their biggest single-day advance in more than two months.

The earnings report prompted positive commentary from Wall Street analysts, with Jefferies upgrading the stock and Wedbush analyst Dan Ives maintaining an Outperform rating.

Jefferies upgrades Rivian stock as R2 targets market gap

Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois upgraded Rivian to Buy from Hold while maintaining a $17 price target. The target implies approximately 45% upside from current levels.

Houchois expects Rivian's R2 electric SUV to benefit as US electric vehicle demand begins to stabilise.

The analyst pointed to what he described as a "relatively unique position and product void" in the 45,000-55,000 price segment.

He sees an opportunity for Rivian between Tesla's increasingly commoditised models and Ford's upcoming electric vehicle based on its Universal Electric Vehicle platform.

However, Ford's new platform may not experience a significant production ramp until late 2027, potentially giving Rivian an opportunity to establish its position in the segment.

Houchois also noted that Rivian shares had corrected roughly 30% over the past three months.

He considers the decline an attractive entry point as the company expands production and explores opportunities to license its autonomous driving technology.

Rivian shares reached approximately $20.20 in July before falling below $12.

Rivian raises 2026 delivery guidance after Q3 earnings beat

Rivian reported third-quarter revenue of $2.16 billion, representing 38% growth from the previous year. Its adjusted loss narrowed to $0.48 per share.

The company also improved its full-year adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) outlook to a loss of $1.75 billion to $1.85 billion.

This represents a $100 million improvement at the midpoint.

Meanwhile, Rivian lowered its capital expenditure guidance to between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion.

The automaker raised its 2026 delivery forecast to 67,000-70,000 vehicles, compared with its previous range of 65,000-70,000.

CEO RJ Scaringe said the R2, which began deliveries in June, had already become the company's best-selling vehicle, outperforming both its R1 models and electric delivery vans.

Rivian has also started a second production shift for the R2 at its Illinois factory.

More affordable versions of the SUV are expected to arrive through late 2026 and 2027.

Dan Ives highlights Rivian's autonomy and software potential

Wedbush analyst Dan Ives maintained an Outperform rating on Rivian with a $20 price target following the quarterly results.

Ives described the report as the "beat-and-raise quarter the R2 story needed", pointing to stronger-than-expected revenue, record deliveries and a narrower loss.

According to Ives, management expects the R2 to help drive the company's automotive business towards positive gross margins by the end of the year.

The revised delivery guidance implies fourth-quarter deliveries of between 25,000 and 28,000 vehicles, the analyst noted.

He also highlighted strong R2 demand and the introduction of a second production shift at Rivian's Normal, Illinois facility.

Beyond vehicle production, Ives pointed to Rivian's software and autonomous driving ambitions, including its joint ventures with Volkswagen and Uber Technologies.

The Uber partnership is expected to unlock another $250 million in equity by the end of the year, supporting a planned 2028 robotaxi launch.

Ives also identified Rivian's AI and self-driving technology as potential catalysts ahead of its December 9 Autonomy and AI Day.

He said these capabilities could represent an area of the business that investors have yet to fully value.

The post Rivian stock rises as analysts back R2 outlook after Q3 earnings beat appeared first on Invezz
